quests.hint: Offer with a question so the person can say yes or no. Mention what you noticed.
quests.explanation: Offering help with a question respects the other person's independence. Noticing a specific detail ('it looks heavy') shows your offer is sincere.
quests.situationText: A woman is pulling a huge suitcase up the station stairs, stopping every few steps to catch her breath.
quests.sampleAnswer: Can I help you carry that up the stairs?
quests.correctAnswer: Would you like a hand with that? It looks heavy.
acceptedSynonyms: Would you like a hand with that? It looks heavy.
Do you need some help with that suitcase? It looks quite heavy.
Can I help you carry that up the stairs?
That looks heavy. Shall I take one end for you?

quests.hint: Offer specific help with a time. Vague offers like 'Let me know if you need anything' rarely get used.
quests.explanation: A specific offer ('I'm free on Saturday') is more useful than a general one, because the friend doesn't have to think of a task or feel guilty asking.
quests.situationText: Your friend Tom mentions that he's moving to a new flat next weekend and hasn't started packing. You're free on Saturday.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm free on Saturday if you want a hand with the packing.
quests.correctAnswer: I'm free on Saturday. Do you want me to help you pack?
acceptedSynonyms: I could come over on Saturday and help you with the boxes, if that's useful.
Would it help if I came on Saturday to help you pack? I'm free all day.
I'm free on Saturday. Do you want me to help you pack?
Let me help. I'm not doing anything on Saturday, so I can pack with you.

quests.hint: Compare 'Can I help?' with 'I know the area'. Saying what you can contribute makes a stranger more willing to accept.
quests.explanation: Saying what you can do ('I know this area well') tells the stranger why your help is worth accepting. It builds trust quickly.
quests.situationText: Two tourists are turning a paper map around in the middle of your street, looking lost. You live here and you're passing by.
quests.sampleAnswer: Are you looking for something? I live around here, so I might be able to help.
quests.correctAnswer: Are you looking for something? I know this area quite well.
acceptedSynonyms: Are you looking for something? I know this area quite well.
You look a bit lost. Can I help? I know the streets here pretty well.
Do you need directions? I've lived here for years.
Sorry to interrupt, but can I help you find anything? I'm local.

quests.hint: Give the date, time, and reason, then ask whether the person is able to. 'Would you be able to…?' gives them an easy way out.
quests.explanation: A favor as big as a lift requires details. 'Would you be able to…?' is softer than 'Can you', because it accepts that the friend may have other plans.
quests.situationText: Your flight leaves at nine on Sunday morning and public transport doesn't start early enough. You ask your friend Ben.
quests.sampleAnswer: Are you free on Sunday morning? I need a ride to the airport for a nine o'clock flight.
quests.correctAnswer: Would you be able to give me a lift to the airport on Sunday morning? My flight is at nine.
acceptedSynonyms: I have a favor to ask. Could you drive me to the airport on Sunday? My flight leaves at nine.
Any chance you could take me to the airport on Sunday morning? I've got a nine o'clock flight.
Would you be able to give me a lift to the airport on Sunday morning? My flight is at nine.
Are you free on Sunday morning? I need a ride to the airport for a nine o'clock flight.

quests.hint: Start with 'Could you do me a favor?' when the favor is a little unusual. State exactly what and when.
quests.explanation: 'Do me a favor' warns the friend that a request is coming, which is friendlier than jumping in. The specific dates make the task clear and finite.
quests.situationText: You're going away for a week and your friend Sara lives close by. You need someone to look after your plants.
quests.sampleAnswer: Are you able to look after my plants for a week? I'm away next week.
quests.correctAnswer: Could you do me a favor and water my plants while I'm away next week?
acceptedSynonyms: Could you do me a favor and water my plants while I'm away next week?
I need a small favor. Would you mind watering my plants next week while I'm away?
Are you able to look after my plants for a week? I'm away next week.
Would you be willing to water my plants while I'm away next week?

quests.hint: Explain why you need it, and make the task small. 'A quick look' feels easier to agree to.
quests.explanation: Requests feel lighter when they seem small. 'Take a quick look' and a clear reason ('to be sure the English is right') invite help without demanding hours.
quests.situationText: You've written your CV in English for a job application, and you're worried about mistakes. Your friend Chris speaks excellent English.
quests.sampleAnswer: Chris, could you take a quick look at my CV? I want to be sure the English is right.
quests.correctAnswer: Could you take a quick look at my CV? I want to make sure the English is correct.
acceptedSynonyms: Would you mind reading through my CV? I'd like to check that my English is right.
I'm applying for a job. Could you check my CV for any mistakes in English?
Could you take a quick look at my CV? I want to make sure the English is correct.
Do you have a few minutes to look over my CV? I just want to be sure the English is right.

quests.hint: Say sorry, name the mistake, and promise a specific fix. A promise with a day is stronger than a vague one.
quests.explanation: A short apology plus a specific solution ('I'll bring it tomorrow') repairs trust. It's better than a long excuse for a small mistake.
quests.situationText: You borrowed a novel from your friend Jo, and she asked you to bring it back today. You forgot it at home.
quests.sampleAnswer: Sorry about that. Your book is still on my desk. I'll bring it in tomorrow.
quests.correctAnswer: Sorry, I forgot to bring your book. I'll bring it tomorrow, I promise.
acceptedSynonyms: I'm really sorry, I left your book at home. I'll definitely bring it tomorrow.
Oh no, I forgot your book. I'll make sure to bring it tomorrow.
Sorry about that. Your book is still on my desk. I'll bring it in tomorrow.
Sorry, I forgot to bring your book. I'll bring it tomorrow, I promise.

quests.hint: If you're late, give the reason and a realistic arrival time. Both help the other person plan.
quests.explanation: Reasons are useful, but a realistic time is essential; it lets your friend decide whether to wait, order, or do something else. 'On my way' shows you're not just apologizing.
quests.situationText: You're meeting a friend for lunch at one o'clock. It's 1:10, and your work meeting is still finishing. You call her. You can be there in about ten minutes.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm so sorry, my meeting overran. I'm leaving now, so about ten minutes.
quests.correctAnswer: Sorry, my meeting ran late. I'm on my way now and I'll be there in ten minutes.
acceptedSynonyms: I'm so sorry, my meeting overran. I'm leaving now, so about ten minutes.
Sorry, my meeting ran late. I'm on my way now and I'll be there in ten minutes.
Sorry I'm late. The meeting went on longer than planned. I'll be with you in ten minutes.
Hi, my meeting isn't finished. I'll leave right now and be there in about ten minutes.

quests.hint: Explain honestly, and show you understand the consequences. That's what makes a team apologize sincerely.
quests.explanation: A good apology to a group acknowledges the effect on others ('let the team down'). The explanation is brief, so the focus stays on responsibility.
quests.situationText: You missed yesterday's football practice because your car broke down. Today you speak to your coach before training starts.
quests.sampleAnswer: Coach, I'm sorry I missed practice yesterday. My car broke down, and I feel bad about letting the team down.
quests.correctAnswer: I couldn't come to practice yesterday because my car broke down. I'm really sorry to let the team down.
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry I wasn't at practice yesterday. My car broke down, and I couldn't get there in time.
I missed practice yesterday because of car trouble. I apologize to you and the team.
My car broke down yesterday, so I couldn't make it to practice. I'm sorry.
I couldn't come to practice yesterday because my car broke down. I'm really sorry to let the team down.

quests.hint: Show you don't completely reject the idea, then suggest an alternative. 'I'm not sure about…' is softer than 'no'.
quests.explanation: 'I'm not sure about' is a soft disagreement. Giving a reason and offering an alternative in the same breath helps the group solve the problem.
quests.situationText: Your friends want to go for Italian food again tonight. You had pizza yesterday and would like something different. You'd like to suggest Thai.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm not sure about Italian. We had pizza yesterday. What about Thai?
quests.correctAnswer: I'm not sure about Italian. I had pizza yesterday. How about Thai?
acceptedSynonyms: Hmm, I had pizza yesterday, so I'd rather not have Italian. Could we try Thai instead?
Italian again? I'm not really in the mood. What about Thai?
I'm not sure about Italian. I had pizza yesterday. How about Thai?
I'd prefer something different tonight. Would anyone like to try a Thai place?

quests.hint: Acknowledge their view before you share yours. 'I see what you mean, but…' keeps things friendly.
quests.explanation: Recognizing the other person's view first shows respect, and 'actually' introduces your different opinion softly. You can disagree without starting an argument.
quests.situationText: A coworker tells you that last night's film was boring. You saw it too and liked it, especially the ending.
quests.sampleAnswer: It was slow in places, I agree, but I liked it in the end.
quests.correctAnswer: I see what you mean, but I actually liked it. I thought the ending was interesting.
acceptedSynonyms: I see what you mean, but I actually liked it. I thought the ending was interesting.
I understand, but I enjoyed it. The ending was great, I thought.
It was slow in places, I agree, but I liked it in the end.
Really? I thought it was good. I especially liked the way it finished.

quests.hint: When you doubt a fact, question it gently and offer to check. This avoids making someone feel wrong.
quests.explanation: 'Are you sure?' is direct, but 'I thought…' softens it and shows you might be wrong. Offering to check the facts turns disagreement into a shared task.
quests.situationText: Your friend says the museum is open on Mondays. You remember reading that it's closed on Mondays and you planned a visit for that day.
quests.sampleAnswer: Are you sure? I thought it was closed on Mondays. Let's check the website.
quests.correctAnswer: Really? I thought the museum was closed on Mondays. Let's check the website.
acceptedSynonyms: I'm not sure that's right. I remember it closing on Mondays. Shall we look it up?
Hmm, I thought it was shut on Mondays. Could we check online to be safe?
Really? I thought the museum was closed on Mondays. Let's check the website.
Are you certain? I read that it's closed on Mondays. Let's double-check.

quests.hint: Give a recommendation with two concrete reasons. Specifics like 'two days' are more convincing than 'it's good'.
quests.explanation: A recommendation is credible when it includes evidence from your own experience. Two reasons, one for each feature, give the person enough to decide.
quests.situationText: Your friend is thinking of buying the same phone you have and asks whether you'd recommend it.
quests.sampleAnswer: Yes, I'd recommend it. The battery lasts two days, and the camera is really good.
quests.correctAnswer: I'd recommend it. The battery lasts two days, and the camera is great.
acceptedSynonyms: Definitely. The battery easily lasts two days, and the photos look fantastic.
I'd go for it. It has a great camera and the battery lasts for two days.
I like mine a lot. The battery is excellent, and the camera is very good.
I'd recommend it. The battery lasts two days, and the camera is great.

quests.hint: A balanced opinion sounds honest. Give a positive, a negative, and your overall view.
quests.explanation: Balanced opinions build trust, because people know you're not simply being polite. 'Though' or 'but' lets you end on the point you most want to be remembered.
quests.situationText: A colleague asks if you've tried the new cafe on the corner. You went last week. The coffee was good, but the place was noisy.
quests.sampleAnswer: I went last week. It's nice, but a bit noisy. The coffee is good, though.
quests.correctAnswer: It's nice, but a bit noisy. The coffee is good though.
acceptedSynonyms: It's decent. The coffee's good, but it gets very noisy.
It's nice, but a bit noisy. The coffee is good though.
I liked the coffee, but the noise level was a bit much.
Not bad. It's loud, but the coffee makes up for it.

quests.hint: Recommend with a condition: if you only have X, I'd do Y. Tourists love a clear priority.
quests.explanation: 'If you only have one day' shows you understand the visitor's limits. A clear top choice with a practical reason is more helpful than a list of ten places.
quests.situationText: A visitor staying in your city for just a day asks what she should see. You think the old town is the best choice.
quests.sampleAnswer: If you've only got one day, I'd go to the old town. It's small enough to walk around.
quests.correctAnswer: If you only have one day, I'd go to the old town. It's small enough to walk around.
acceptedSynonyms: With just one day, I'd suggest the old town. You can see most of it on foot.
I'd spend the day in the old town. It's compact, so you can walk everywhere.
If time is short, the old town is your best choice. It's easy to cover on foot.
If you only have one day, I'd go to the old town. It's small enough to walk around.

quests.hint: Show real happiness and add a comment about why they deserve it.
quests.explanation: Congratulations sound warmer when you add a reason. 'You really deserved it' shows you know about the person's effort, not only the result.
quests.situationText: Your friend Daria has just told you she got the job she interviewed for last week after months of searching.
quests.sampleAnswer: Congratulations! That's fantastic news. You really deserved it.
quests.correctAnswer: Congratulations, that's fantastic news! You really deserve it.
acceptedSynonyms: Oh, well done! I'm so happy for you. All your hard work paid off.
Congratulations, that's fantastic news! You really deserve it.
That's brilliant news, Daria! You worked so hard for it.
Wow, congratulations! I'm thrilled for you. You earned it.

quests.hint: For sad news, express sympathy first, then offer support. Don't rush to give solutions.
quests.explanation: Sympathy comes before help. 'I'm so sorry to hear that' acknowledges the feeling, and the offer that follows lets the friend decide whether they want support.
quests.situationText: Your friend Tariq tells you that his grandfather died last week. He looks very tired.
quests.sampleAnswer: That's so sad. I'm really sorry, Tariq. I'm here if you want to talk.
quests.correctAnswer: I'm so sorry to hear that. Is there anything I can do?
acceptedSynonyms: I'm very sorry for your loss. Please tell me if there's anything I can do.
That's so sad. I'm really sorry, Tariq. I'm here if you want to talk.
I'm so sorry. Let me know if I can help in any way.
I'm so sorry to hear that. Is there anything I can do?

quests.hint: For a minor problem, keep the sympathy light and give a wish. 'I hope you feel better soon' is standard.
quests.explanation: A short wish is enough for a common illness. Overly dramatic sympathy for a cold can feel strange, so match your reaction to the size of the problem.
quests.situationText: A coworker comes in with a red nose, coughing, and tells you she's had the flu all weekend.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh no, poor you. I hope you feel better soon.
quests.correctAnswer: Oh no, that sounds awful. I hope you feel better soon.
acceptedSynonyms: That's horrible. Go home and rest if you can. Get well soon.
Oh no, that sounds awful. I hope you feel better soon.
Sorry to hear that. Take care of yourself, and I hope it passes quickly.
You poor thing. Make sure you rest and get better soon.

quests.hint: A good host does three things at the door: welcome, take something, and offer a drink. Keep sentences short.
quests.explanation: Hosts help the guest feel comfortable quickly. Taking a coat and offering a drink are automatic gestures, and short sentences keep the greeting warm.
quests.situationText: Your friend Nina arrives at your flat for dinner, holding a bunch of flowers and wearing a heavy coat.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, Nina, great to see you! Let me take that coat. What would you like to drink?
quests.correctAnswer: Come in! Let me take your coat. Can I get you something to drink?
acceptedSynonyms: Come in! Let me take your coat. Can I get you something to drink?
Welcome! Please, come in. Can I take your coat? Would you like a drink?
Hi, Nina, great to see you! Let me take that coat. What would you like to drink?
Come on in, Nina. Give me your coat. Would you like tea, or something cold?

quests.hint: As a guest, mention what you brought and ask where to put it. It's a friendly way to hand over a gift.
quests.explanation: Asking where to put the gift lets the host guide you. Mentioning what it is ('cake for dessert') lets them plan the meal.
quests.situationText: You arrive at your colleague's house for dinner with a homemade cake in a box. She opens the door.
quests.sampleAnswer: I made a cake for after dinner. Where would you like it?
quests.correctAnswer: I brought some cake for dessert. Where should I put it?
acceptedSynonyms: I made a cake for after dinner. Where would you like it?
Here's a cake I baked for dessert. Where can I put it?
I brought some cake for dessert. Where should I put it?
I brought a little something for dessert. Should I put it in the kitchen?

quests.hint: If you want more, accept and give a small compliment. If the amount is small, say so.
quests.explanation: Accepting food with 'yes, please' and a compliment makes the host feel appreciated. Saying 'just a small piece' is a polite way to control the portion.
quests.situationText: At a dinner party, your host asks if you'd like another slice of apple pie. You'd love one, but you're nearly full.
quests.sampleAnswer: Yes, please, just a small piece. It's really good.
quests.correctAnswer: Yes, please. Just a small slice. It's really good.
acceptedSynonyms: Yes, please. Just a small slice. It's really good.
I'd love some more, thank you, but only a little. It's delicious.
Go on then, a small piece. It's lovely.
Yes, thanks, just a little bit. This pie is fantastic.

quests.hint: Say hello and connect the conversation to your mutual friend. It gives you both something to talk about.
quests.explanation: 'How do you know Elena?' is the classic question at parties because your mutual friend is the one thing you both have in common at that moment.
quests.situationText: At a birthday party, your friend Elena introduces you to her friend Pablo and then goes to get drinks, leaving the two of you together.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi Pablo, good to meet you. Have you and Elena been friends for a long time?
quests.correctAnswer: Nice to meet you, Pablo. How do you know Elena?
acceptedSynonyms: Good to meet you, Pablo. How did you and Elena meet?
Hi Pablo, nice to meet you. How do you two know each other?
Nice to meet you, Pablo. How do you know Elena?
Pleased to meet you. Are you and Elena old friends?

quests.hint: Show that you've heard good things about the person, and mention one specific detail.
quests.explanation: Saying 'Elena's told me about you' makes the person feel welcome. A specific detail, like the piano, proves that it wasn't a generic compliment.
quests.situationText: At a dinner, your friend Elena introduces you to Maya, someone you've never met, but you've heard she plays the piano.
quests.sampleAnswer: Elena's told me a lot about you. She said you play the piano.
quests.correctAnswer: I've heard a lot about you from Elena. She says you play the piano.
acceptedSynonyms: I've heard a lot about you from Elena. She says you play the piano.
Elena has mentioned you many times. I hear you play the piano.
So you're Maya! Elena told me you're a pianist.
Elena talks about you a lot. She said you play the piano beautifully.

quests.hint: Joining a group takes courtesy: apologize for interrupting and ask a question so they can include you.
quests.explanation: 'Sorry to jump in' acknowledges that you're interrupting, and asking what the topic is lets the group welcome you. It's better than standing awkwardly listening.
quests.situationText: At a networking event, three people are laughing together. You know none of them, but the conversation looks friendly and you'd like to join.
quests.sampleAnswer: Sorry to jump in. What are you all talking about?
quests.correctAnswer: Sorry to interrupt. Do you mind if I join you? It looks like a fun conversation.
acceptedSynonyms: Hi, do you mind if I join you? It sounds like you're having fun.
Sorry for barging in. Can I join you? What's the joke?
Sorry to interrupt. Do you mind if I join you? It looks like a fun conversation.
Hello, may I join you? You all look like you're having a great time.

quests.hint: React with surprise first, then ask a question that shows interest. Match the energy of the news.
quests.explanation: When someone shares big news, an emotional reaction ('Wow') comes before practical questions. Then 'When are you leaving?' shows that you're curious about the details.
quests.situationText: Your friend Rina suddenly says she's accepted a job in Canada and will move in two months. You had no idea.
quests.sampleAnswer: Wow, I didn't expect that! When are you leaving?
quests.correctAnswer: Wow, I didn't see that coming! When are you leaving?
acceptedSynonyms: No way! That's a big surprise. When do you go?
Really? That's huge news! When are you moving?
Oh my goodness, I had no idea. When do you leave?
Wow, I didn't see that coming! When are you leaving?

quests.hint: Show sympathy for bad news and ask what's next. That's more helpful than only saying 'that's too bad.'
quests.explanation: 'What are you going to do?' shows you care about what happens next. It also allows the person to talk about the problem and their options.
quests.situationText: A coworker tells you her flight to a family wedding has been cancelled and the next one is two days later.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh no, that's awful. What are you going to do?
quests.correctAnswer: Oh no, that's terrible. What are you going to do now?
acceptedSynonyms: That's so annoying! Have you looked at other flights yet?
Oh no, that's terrible. What are you going to do now?
Oh dear. Will you still be able to go to the wedding?
That's the worst. Do you know what your options are?

quests.hint: Strong feelings need more than one word. Combine your surprise with a real thank-you.
quests.explanation: A strong emotion deserves more than one word. Disbelief plus thanks shows you noticed the effort, which is what your friends want from a surprise party.
quests.situationText: You walk into your flat after work and all your friends jump out shouting 'Happy birthday!' You had no idea about the party.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh my goodness! I can't believe you did this. Thank you all so much!
quests.correctAnswer: I can't believe you did all this! Thank you so much, everyone.
acceptedSynonyms: Wow, what a surprise! I had no idea. You're the best, thank you!
I'm speechless! Thank you all for doing this for me.
You got me completely! This is so kind of you all. Thank you.
I can't believe you did all this! Thank you so much, everyone.

quests.hint: Show you liked both ideas, then combine them. Compromise begins with acceptance.
quests.explanation: Compromise sounds friendly when you show that you like each person's idea first. Proposing to do both at different times lets everyone win.
quests.situationText: Five friends are planning a holiday. Two want the beach and two want the mountains. They look at you to decide.
quests.sampleAnswer: I like both ideas. Could we do the beach this time and the mountains next time?
quests.correctAnswer: I like both ideas. Could we do the beach for a weekend and the mountains next time?
acceptedSynonyms: Both sound great. What if we go to the beach now and save the mountains for later?
I like both ideas. Could we do the beach for a weekend and the mountains next time?
Why don't we do a bit of both? Beach this summer, mountains in the autumn?
I'd be happy with either. Maybe we can take turns: beach first, then mountains.

quests.hint: Find a solution that helps the person who has a problem. Suggest a change and give the benefit.
quests.explanation: Presenting a change with its benefit ('those who finish late can still make it') makes it feel like a service to the group instead of a complaint.
quests.situationText: Your friends planned to meet at five, but two of them finish work at 5:30 and keep arriving late. You suggest a different time. You'd like to suggest six o'clock.
quests.sampleAnswer: What if we met at six instead? Then people who finish late can still make it.
quests.correctAnswer: How about we meet at six instead? That way, those who finish late can still make it.
acceptedSynonyms: Could we make it six o'clock? Then nobody has to rush from work.
Shall we move it to six? That would help the people who finish late.
Would six work better? It gives the late finishers time to get there.
How about we meet at six instead? That way, those who finish late can still make it.

quests.hint: Share the responsibility fairly. Offer your part and ask if the group agrees.
quests.explanation: Splitting a task fairly is easier when you offer first. Ending with a check-in question ('Does that work?') invites the group to agree or adjust.
quests.situationText: Four friends are going to a lake three hours away. Nobody wants to drive both ways, and someone has to decide.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'll drive there if someone else can drive back. Does that work for everyone?
quests.correctAnswer: I'm happy to drive there if someone else drives back. Does that work for everyone?
acceptedSynonyms: I can drive on the way there, but I'd like someone else to take the way home. Is that fair?
I'm happy to drive there if someone else drives back. Does that work for everyone?
How about I take the first half and someone else does the return trip? What do you think?
I'll do the drive there. Could somebody else drive us back?
